blocks.text: A 68-year-old man wakes after repair of a ruptured aortic aneurysm unable to move his legs and unable to feel pin-prick or temperature below the chest. Remarkably, he can still sense vibration and the position of his toes. A cord only about one centimetre wide is organised so precisely that different functions can be lost independently.

blocks.markdown:
In cross-section the spinal cord has an inner **grey matter** in the shape of a butterfly or letter H, surrounded by **white matter** made of ascending and descending tracts. The grey matter has a **dorsal (posterior) horn** (sensory processing), a **ventral (anterior) horn** (alpha and gamma motor neurones), and, from **T1 to L2**, a **lateral horn** containing the sympathetic preganglionic neurones (with a parasympathetic equivalent at S2-S4). The **central canal** lies at the centre. The white matter is divided into **dorsal, lateral and ventral funiculi**.

**The three tracts to identify:**

- **Dorsal columns** (**fasciculus gracilis** medially, from the lower body, and **fasciculus cuneatus** laterally, from the upper body above T6) lie in the **dorsal funiculus** between the dorsal horns. They carry fine touch, vibration and proprioception, **ipsilaterally**.
- **Spinothalamic tract** (anterolateral system) lies in the **anterolateral** white matter, at the border between lateral and ventral funiculi. It carries pain, temperature and crude touch from the **opposite** side of the body.
- **Lateral corticospinal tract** lies in the **lateral funiculus**, deep in the posterior part next to the dorsal horn. It carries voluntary motor commands to alpha motor neurones of the **same side** of the body below the decussation.

rows: In the cord, within one or two segments of entry (anterior white commissure)
Caudal medulla (pyramidal decussation), about 85-90% of fibres

blocks.title: Identifying a tract from a lesion on a cross-section
blocks.prompt: On a cord cross-section at T8, a lesion destroys the right lateral funiculus (posterior part) only. Which tract is affected, and what deficit is expected?

steps.text: The posterior part of the lateral funiculus contains the lateral corticospinal tract.
Its fibres have already decussated in the medulla, so the right tract controls the right side of the body.
A lesion produces an upper motor neurone weakness of the right leg below T8 (spasticity, brisk reflexes, extensor plantar response).

blocks.answer: The right lateral corticospinal tract: right-sided UMN weakness below the lesion.

blocks.markdown:
**Where each tract crosses (decussation).**

- **Dorsal column pathway**: first-order fibres ascend uncrossed to the **nucleus gracilis or cuneatus** in the caudal medulla; second-order fibres **decussate in the medulla** as the internal arcuate fibres and ascend as the medial lemniscus. A cord lesion therefore causes **ipsilateral** loss.
- **Spinothalamic tract**: first-order fibres synapse in the dorsal horn; second-order fibres **cross in the anterior white commissure within one or two segments** of entry and ascend contralaterally. A cord lesion causes **contralateral** loss beginning one or two segments below the lesion.
- **Corticospinal tract**: the fibres descend through the internal capsule and brainstem and, in the **caudal medulla (pyramidal decussation)**, about 85-90% cross to form the **lateral corticospinal tract**. The remaining 10-15% descend uncrossed as the **anterior corticospinal tract** and cross at their level of termination. A cord lesion causes **ipsilateral** motor weakness.

blocks.title: A right hemisection at T8
blocks.prompt: Predict the motor and sensory deficits below a right-sided hemisection of the cord at T8.

steps.text: Right lateral corticospinal tract (already crossed above): ipsilateral right leg UMN weakness.
Right dorsal column (uncrossed in the cord): ipsilateral right loss of vibration and proprioception.

Spinothalamic fibres from the left leg cross in the cord below the lesion and ascend on the right, so they are interrupted: contralateral left loss of pain and temperature, starting a segment or two below T8.

blocks.answer: Right leg weakness and loss of vibration and proprioception; left loss of pain and temperature below the lesion.

blocks.markdown:
**Blood supply of the spinal cord.** The cord is supplied by longitudinal arteries reinforced by segmental arteries.

- A single **anterior spinal artery** (formed from branches of the two vertebral arteries) runs in the anterior median fissure and supplies the **anterior two thirds** of the cord: the ventral horns, the spinothalamic tracts, and the corticospinal tracts.
- Two **posterior spinal arteries** (from the vertebral or posterior inferior cerebellar arteries) supply the **posterior third**: the dorsal columns and dorsal horns.
- **Segmental (radicular) arteries** from the aorta reinforce these longitudinal vessels. The largest, the **great anterior radicular artery (artery of Adamkiewicz)**, usually arises from the lower thoracic or upper lumbar region (commonly on the left) and supplies much of the lower cord. The thoracic region is a **vulnerable watershed** with relatively poor supply.

**Anterior spinal artery occlusion** (aortic surgery, dissection, severe hypotension) causes infarction of the anterior two thirds: **loss of motor function below the lesion** (UMN signs, often flaccid in the acute phase) and **loss of pain and temperature sensation** below the lesion, **bilaterally**, with **preservation of dorsal column function** (vibration, proprioception, fine touch). Bladder and bowel control are usually lost.

rows: Anterior two thirds: ventral horns, spinothalamic, corticospinal tracts
Bilateral motor loss and loss of pain and temperature below the level; dorsal columns spared
Posterior third: dorsal columns and horns
Infarction of the lower cord, an anterior spinal syndrome

blocks.title: What anterior spinal infarction spares
blocks.text: The dorsal columns are supplied by the posterior spinal arteries, so vibration and proprioception are spared when the anterior spinal artery is occluded.

items: The spinal cord ends at the conus medullaris, around the level of the L1-L2 vertebrae in adults; below this the nerve roots form the cauda equina.
Cord segments are numbered by the spinal nerves they give rise to, and do not match vertebral levels below the cervical region.
The dorsal horn receives sensory afferents; the ventral horn contains the motor neurones whose axons form the ventral roots.

points: The cord has dorsal, ventral and (T1-L2) lateral horns; the dorsal columns, spinothalamic and lateral corticospinal tracts occupy the dorsal, anterolateral and lateral white matter respectively.
Dorsal column fibres cross in the medulla, spinothalamic fibres cross in the cord within one or two segments, and about 85-90% of corticospinal fibres cross at the pyramidal decussation.
One anterior spinal artery supplies the anterior two thirds of the cord and two posterior spinal arteries the posterior third; anterior spinal artery occlusion spares the dorsal columns.

questions.stem: In which part of the spinal cord white matter do the fasciculus gracilis and cuneatus lie?

distractorRationale.b: The ventral funiculus contains anterior corticospinal and other tracts.
distractorRationale.c: The anterolateral region holds the spinothalamic tract.
distractorRationale.d: The anterior white commissure carries crossing spinothalamic fibres.

questions.explanation: The fasciculus gracilis and fasciculus cuneatus form the dorsal columns in the dorsal funiculus between the dorsal horns. They carry fine touch, vibration and proprioception.

questions.stem: Where in the cord cross-section is the lateral corticospinal tract found?

options.text: Lateral funiculus, deep and posterior, next to the dorsal horn
Next to the anterior median fissure

questions.correctOptionText: Lateral funiculus, deep and posterior, next to the dorsal horn

distractorRationale.b: The dorsal funiculus holds the dorsal columns.
distractorRationale.c: The anterior corticospinal tract lies near the anterior median fissure.
distractorRationale.d: The dorsal horn is grey matter.

questions.explanation: The lateral corticospinal tract lies in the lateral funiculus, posterior and deep, adjacent to the dorsal horn.

questions.stem: Which spinal cord segments contain the lateral horn with sympathetic preganglionic neurones?

distractorRationale.b: The cervical cord has no sympathetic lateral horn.
distractorRationale.c: These segments have no lateral horn.

questions.explanation: The lateral horn, which houses sympathetic preganglionic cell bodies, is present from T1 to L2 (the thoracolumbar outflow).

questions.stem: At what level do the second-order fibres of the dorsal column pathway decussate?

options.text: In the spinal cord, near their level of entry
In the caudal medulla (internal arcuate fibres)

questions.correctOptionText: In the caudal medulla (internal arcuate fibres)

distractorRationale.c: No major sensory decussation occurs in the midbrain for this pathway.
distractorRationale.d: The thalamus is a relay, not a site of crossing.

questions.explanation: Dorsal column fibres ascend ipsilaterally to the medulla, synapse in the gracile and cuneate nuclei, and the second-order fibres cross as internal arcuate fibres.

questions.stem: What proportion of corticospinal fibres cross at the pyramidal decussation to form the lateral corticospinal tract?

distractorRationale.a: That is the proportion that stays uncrossed.
distractorRationale.d: The majority do cross in the caudal medulla.

questions.explanation: Roughly 85-90% of corticospinal fibres decussate in the caudal medulla and form the lateral corticospinal tract. The remainder form the anterior corticospinal tract, which crosses at the segmental level.

questions.stem: Spinothalamic second-order neurones decussate at which site?

options.text: Anterior white commissure, within one or two segments of entry

questions.correctOptionText: Anterior white commissure, within one or two segments of entry

distractorRationale.a: Medullary crossing applies to the dorsal column pathway.
distractorRationale.c: No sensory decussation occurs here for this pathway.
distractorRationale.d: They do cross, giving contralateral loss.

questions.explanation: Spinothalamic second-order fibres cross in the anterior white commissure close to their level of entry and ascend on the opposite side.

questions.stem: True or false: the anterior spinal artery supplies the dorsal columns.
questions.explanation: The dorsal columns are supplied by the paired posterior spinal arteries. The anterior spinal artery supplies the anterior two thirds of the cord.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman suffers prolonged severe hypotension after a cardiac arrest, causing infarction of the anterior spinal artery territory at about T8. Which findings are expected below the lesion?

options.text: Bilateral leg weakness and loss of pain and temperature with preserved vibration and proprioception
Bilateral loss of vibration and proprioception with preserved strength and pain sensation
Right-sided weakness and left-sided loss of vibration only
Isolated loss of bladder function with normal limbs

questions.correctOptionText: Bilateral leg weakness and loss of pain and temperature with preserved vibration and proprioception

distractorRationale.a: Correct: corticospinal and spinothalamic tracts infarct; dorsal columns are spared.
distractorRationale.b: This is the reverse pattern, from posterior spinal artery or dorsal column disease.
distractorRationale.c: A unilateral pattern would indicate a hemicord lesion.

questions.explanation: Anterior spinal artery occlusion infarcts the anterior two thirds of the cord, which contains the corticospinal and spinothalamic tracts. The dorsal columns, supplied by the posterior spinal arteries, are spared.

questions.stem: Explain why the mid-thoracic region of the spinal cord is vulnerable to ischaemia, describing the arterial supply, and predict the effects of occlusion of the anterior spinal artery in this region.
markingGuide: A single anterior spinal artery supplies the anterior two thirds; two posterior spinal arteries supply the posterior third
Longitudinal arteries are reinforced by segmental (radicular) arteries
The thoracic cord has relatively few reinforcing vessels and is a watershed region
The great anterior radicular artery (Adamkiewicz) usually arises in the lower thoracic or upper lumbar region and supplies the lower cord
Occlusion: bilateral motor loss (corticospinal) and loss of pain and temperature (spinothalamic) below the level, with preserved dorsal column function
Bladder and bowel dysfunction may occur
questions.explanation: The cord relies on a few reinforcing segmental arteries, and the thoracic region is a watershed with a precarious supply. Anterior spinal infarction therefore causes loss of motor and spinothalamic function below the level, with the dorsal columns spared.

questions.stem: Describe the position of the dorsal column, spinothalamic and lateral corticospinal tracts on a cord cross-section, and state where each decussates.
markingGuide: Dorsal columns lie in the dorsal funiculus (gracilis medial, cuneatus lateral)
Lateral corticospinal tract lies in the lateral funiculus, posterior part
Dorsal column pathway decussates in the caudal medulla
Spinothalamic fibres decussate in the cord (anterior white commissure) within one or two segments
Corticospinal fibres (about 85-90%) decussate at the pyramidal decussation in the caudal medulla
questions.explanation: Because each tract crosses at a different level, a lesion in the cord produces ipsilateral dorsal column and corticospinal signs but contralateral spinothalamic signs. Knowing the positions and decussation levels is the basis of cord localisation.
